title: Flemings Left Hand Rule: Simple Guide With 5 Easy Examples
text:
Electrical Fundamentals

 Fleming's Left Hand Rule: Simple Guide With 5 Easy Examples

 Put a wire carrying current inside a magnetic field and it gets pushed sideways, which is the effect that spins every electric motor. Three fingers of your left hand tell you exactly which way that push acts, before you write a single equation.

 
 Motor Rule 
 Thumb Force 
 Forefinger Field 
 Middle Finger Current 
 F = BIL sin θ 
 




 A current carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force, and its direction decides which way a motor turns. A simple three finger trick finds that direction, while F = BIL sin θ gives its size.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn Flemings left hand rule, how the thumb, forefinger and middle finger show force, field and current, and how F = BIL sin θ gives the force inside motors.


 
 
 
 What Is Fleming's Left Hand Rule?


 Fleming's left hand rule is a memory aid that gives the direction of the force on a current carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field. It applies to motor action, where electrical energy becomes motion, and it is the starting point for understanding every DC motor .


 Hold the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually at right angles. The forefinger points along the magnetic field from north to south, the middle finger along the conventional current, and the thumb then shows the force or motion.



 
 
 



 The British engineer John Ambrose Fleming created the left and right hand rules in the late 19th century. His aim was to help students tell motor action apart from generator action, a confusion that still trips up many learners today.


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 The Three Fingers and What They Mean


 
 Thumb
 Points in the direction of the force, thrust or motion of the conductor.
 Best for: motion of the wire or rotor
 Force F 

 Forefinger
 Points along the magnetic field, from the north pole toward the south pole.
 Best for: field of magnet or stator
 Field B 

 Middle Finger
 Points along the conventional current, from positive to negative.
 Best for: current in the conductor
 Current I 




 A popular way to remember the order is FBI. The thumb is Force, the forefinger is the B field and the middle finger is the current I, reading from the top finger down.


 Do You Know?
 Fleming also invented the thermionic valve, or vacuum diode, in 1904. That one device opened the road to radio and early electronics.



 NCERT introduces Fleming's left hand rule in the Class 10 Science chapter on Magnetic Effects of Electric Current, right after the experiment where a rod in a horseshoe magnet jumps when current flows. That same chapter recalls that Oersted discovered in 1820 that a current deflects a compass needle.


 Force on a Conductor: F = BIL sin θ


 The finger rule gives direction only, so the size of the force needs a formula. Electrical4U gives it as F = BIL sin θ, where θ is the angle between the current and the field.


 
 F = B × I × L × sin θ 

F = force on the conductor in newton
B = magnetic flux density in tesla
I = current in ampere
L = length of conductor inside the field in metre

Example:
B = 0.5 T, I = 10 A, L = 0.2 m, θ = 90°
F = 0.5 × 10 × 0.2 × sin 90°
 F = 1 × 1 = 1.000 N 



 The force is largest when the current crosses the field at 90°, because sin 90° equals 1. Electrical4U points out that the force becomes zero when the current runs parallel to the field, since sin 0° equals 0.


 Each quantity uses its SI unit, and the tesla, ampere and newton are explained in electrical units of measure . Doubling any one of B, I or L doubles the force, which is why motors use strong magnets, many turns and long active conductors.

 Quick Tip
 Enter the angle between the wire and the field, not between the wire and the magnet face. A wire running straight along the field lines feels no force at all.

 How to Apply the Rule Step by Step


 
 1
 Find the Field
 Mark the field from the north pole to the south pole.


 2
 Find the Current
 Mark conventional current from positive to negative.


 3
 Set the Fingers
 Point forefinger along the field and middle finger along the current.


 4
 Read the Thumb
 The thumb now points along the force on the conductor.





 Try it on a horizontal wire between magnet poles, with north on the left and south on the right, and current flowing away from you into the page. Your forefinger points right, your middle finger points away, and your thumb points upward, so the wire is pushed up.


 Reverse either the current or the field and the force reverses. Reverse both together and the force stays the same, which is why a DC series motor keeps turning in the same direction even when the supply polarity is swapped.


 Second Worked Example: Torque on a Motor Coil


 A rectangular coil of 50 turns sits in a 0.4 T field and carries 2 A. Each active side is 0.05 m long and the two sides are 0.04 m apart.


 
 Force on one side = N × B × I × L 
 Torque = Force × coil width 

Force = 50 × 0.4 × 2 × 0.05 = 2 N
Torque = 2 × 0.04
 Torque = 0.08 N m 



 Fleming's left hand rule shows that the two sides are pushed in opposite directions, because their currents flow opposite ways in the same field. The two forces form a couple that turns the coil, and a commutator reverses the current every half turn so the torque keeps the same sense.
